learningObjectives: Build a Requirements structure using Folders, RequirementSets, and layered Requirements.
Apply Basic Weighting to indicate the relative importance of a Requirement.
Calculate a weight from Frequency class and Damage class using the documented base-2 formula.
Distinguish relative weighting, contribution, execution coverage and execution state.
Refresh Requirement values using manual updates or AutoCalculateRequirements.

elements.description: A criterion the system under test is expected to fulfil — functional (e.g. 'a customer can pay with a Visa card') or non-functional (e.g. system security). Requirements are gathered from workshops with stakeholders, or from existing specs/BA documents.

elements.title: Structural hierarchy, top to bottom
items: Folder — organizes the Requirements section, usually mirroring the system or process structure; can be nested.
RequirementSet — sits inside a Folder; groups Requirements representing one aspect of the application (frontend, backend, non-functional) or one process view (a sprint, a regression cycle).
Requirement — created inside a RequirementSet; can contain sub-Requirements, forming layers.

Leaf Requirement — the lowest-level criterion in your design. Independent recommendation: keep each criterion understandable and traceable; the documentation does not prescribe one universal user-story size.

elements.description: Independent design recommendation: organize broad areas and refine only as needed for traceability. A readable hierarchy helps navigation; depth alone does not establish more accurate coverage.

elements.text: In current documentation, create a folder from a Requirements folder and create a RequirementSet within it. Select Create Requirement on the RequirementSet mini toolbar. Requirement types beyond the default can be configured by administrators.

bulletPoints: Same structure order every time: Folder → RequirementSet → Requirement → (optional) sub-Requirements.
Independent Agile organization example: use sprint-oriented groups when they support your reporting needs; this is not a mandatory Tosca structure.

elements.description: New Requirements have weight 1. Set weights with stakeholders to express relative business risk; the Weight column contains those values. Do not confuse direct weights with the 0–10 input scale documented for Frequency class and Damage class.
Independent planning technique: agree on broad business areas before detailed criteria so priorities are consistent. This is a suggested workflow, not an enforced Tosca entry order.

bulletPoints: Default weight is 1. A simple agreed scale is an independent team convention, not a documented mandatory 1–5 best practice.
Frequency and Damage class use a documented 0–10 scale; the directly entered Weight is a different value.

elements.description: A single linear scale often can't distinguish importance clearly enough (is this a 3 or a 4?). Complex Weighting instead asks two separate business questions per Requirement and lets Tosca calculate the Weight for you.

elements.title: The two input values
items: Frequency Class — 'How often is this functionality used?'
Damage Class — 'How much financial damage would we incur if this functionality failed?'

elements.description: The 2024.1 column reference documents Weight = 2^Frequency class × 2^Damage class; each class ranges from 0 to 10. For Frequency 3 and Damage 2, the result is 8 × 4 = 32. These are relative risk estimates, not exact monetary predictions.

elements.text: Independent planning recommendation: discuss frequency and damage estimates with business stakeholders and apply the agreed scale consistently.

bulletPoints: Multiply the two powers of 2; multiplying the input class numbers alone is not the formula.
Both values are estimates for comparison purposes, not precise financial figures.

elements.description: The 2024.1 reference describes Contribution (%) as a Requirement’s weighted share of its RequirementSet, with sub-Requirements calculated relative to their parent. Contribution is an importance allocation, not proof that tests passed.

The reference defines Relative Weight (%) as the Requirement weight divided by the total RequirementSet weight. For a flat set with positive total weight, the percentages sum to 100. Do not treat this as an unconditional rule for every level, filtered view or zero-total-weight structure.

Link TestCases to Requirements directly or through TestCase Links. Reporting distinguishes completed specification, executed tests and pass/fail state. Execution State also depends on result aggregation, which the 2024.1 reference says defaults to First. TestCase Design Coverage is separate and independent of Weight and WorkState.

bulletPoints: Coverage Executed includes both passed and failed tests; it does not mean all executed tests passed.
Coverage Specified considers completed WorkState and links; TestCase Design Coverage answers a different question.

elements.description: Tosca On-Premises 2026.1 documents AutoCalculateRequirements as off by default. A linked test change can leave calculated Requirement values outdated; the blue exclamation indicator identifies stale RequirementSets.
Right-click a RequirementSet and choose Update Outdated Values, or use Update Outdated Values in the Requirements dynamic menu to recalculate all outdated values.

elements.text: Enable AutoCalculateRequirements under Project → Settings → Commander → General → Advanced, then restart Tosca. Automatic recalculation can cause considerable waits in large repositories.

Independent Quilyn notes use the public documentation below. The authenticated Academy videos and exercise files were not accessible, so historical version transitions and exercise numbering are not certified here.

bulletPoints: Current baseline: 2026.1 updates are manual by default; changing automatic-calculation settings requires a restart.

examPitfalls.title: Treating Complex Weighting as additive
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming Weight = Frequency Class + Damage Class.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: With the documented base-2 formula, multiply 2^Frequency by 2^Damage. Input classes and the resulting Weight are different quantities.

examPitfalls.title: Mixing up Contribution (%) and Relative Weight (%)
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Confusing risk importance with executed/pass coverage, or claiming every hierarchy level always totals 100%.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Relative Weight compares with RequirementSet total weight; Contribution uses parent context for sub-Requirements. Separate those allocations from execution and specification metrics.

examPitfalls.title: Expecting immediate updates with default settings
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Making a change elsewhere in the project and expecting the Requirements dashboard to reflect it immediately, then reporting stale numbers.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: In 2026.1, refresh outdated values manually or enable AutoCalculateRequirements and restart. Do not certify historical release transitions from current documentation.

examPitfalls.title: Treating a suggested weighting workflow as mandatory
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming Tosca enforces top-down entry or a universal 1–5 weighting policy.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Agree on a consistent business-risk model. Top-down discussion is an independent planning suggestion, not a product restriction.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the correct structural order when building a Requirements tree in Tosca, from top to bottom?
practiceQuiz.hint: Folders organize the section; RequirementSets group Requirements by aspect or process view; Requirements can then be layered.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The structure is always Folder → RequirementSet → Requirement, with Requirements optionally containing sub-Requirements down to Leaf Requirements.

optionExplanations.A: RequirementSets are inside folders, not containers above them.
optionExplanations.B: The documented containers run from folder to set to Requirement.
optionExplanations.C: A Requirement is not the outer folder container.
optionExplanations.D: A RequirementSet groups Requirements, not the reverse.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Requirement has a Frequency Class of 3 and a Damage Class of 2. Using the default base value of 2, how is its Complex Weight calculated?
practiceQuiz.hint: Complex Weighting is exponential, not additive — each class is raised to the power of the base value.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The formula is Weight = 2^(Frequency Class) × 2^(Damage Class), so 2^3 × 2^2 = 8 × 4 = 32. The exponential nature spreads Requirements apart more clearly than a simple sum would.

optionExplanations.A: Adding the input classes does not apply the exponential formula.
optionExplanations.B: 8 multiplied by 4 is 32, matching the documented formula.
optionExplanations.C: Multiplying raw classes omits the powers of 2.
optionExplanations.D: The extra division by 2 is not part of the formula.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In a flat RequirementSet with a positive total weight, which statement correctly describes the weight-related reporting columns?

options.text: Relative Weight (%) compares each weight to the RequirementSet total; Contribution (%) represents weighted share, with parent context for sub-Requirements.
Contribution (%) and Relative Weight (%) both show the percentage of tests that passed.
Relative Weight (%) is based only on execution duration.
They are two different names for the same calculated value.

practiceQuiz.hint: Importance allocations and execution outcomes are different metrics.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The reference defines Relative Weight relative to the RequirementSet total and Contribution as a weighted contribution, with parent-relative calculation for sub-Requirements. Neither column is a pass-rate metric; for a flat structure their values can coincide.

optionExplanations.A: The two columns describe weighting, with parent context for nested contribution.
optionExplanations.B: Passed-test coverage is not the meaning of either weight column.
optionExplanations.C: Execution duration is unrelated to this weight percentage.
optionExplanations.D: They can coincide in a flat structure but their documented meanings differ.

practiceQuiz.scenario: In Tosca On-Premises 2026.1, a new TestCase link is added but calculated Requirement values remain outdated. What should the tester check?

options.text: Requirements never update automatically in any Tosca version; a full project reload is required.
AutoCalculateRequirements is off by default; use Update Outdated Values, or enable it and restart Tosca.
TestCases cannot be linked to Requirements at all.
The Weight formula needs to be recalculated manually every time.

practiceQuiz.hint: Look for the exclamation mark next to the RequirementSet — that's the tell.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The current documentation states that automatic calculation is off by default. Recalculate the flagged RequirementSet manually or enable AutoCalculateRequirements under the documented settings path and restart; no full project reload is required for a manual update.

optionExplanations.A: Manual update does not require a complete reload; automatic calculation is configurable.
optionExplanations.B: Default-off calculation, manual refresh and a restart after setting changes match the current documentation.
optionExplanations.C: The documentation explicitly supports linking tests to Requirements.
optionExplanations.D: Risk-weight arithmetic alone does not refresh all linked reporting values.

quickRecap.value: Folder → RequirementSet → Requirement → (optional) sub-Requirements, down to Leaf Requirements.
Default Weight is 1. Agree on a consistent risk scale; 0–10 applies to Frequency and Damage class inputs.
Weighted contribution to the RequirementSet; sub-Requirements are calculated relative to their parent, not a pass-rate metric.
Weight relative to the RequirementSet total; flat positive-total structures sum to 100%.
2026.1: manual by default. Update Outdated Values or enable AutoCalculateRequirements and restart Tosca.
